title: 3 Simple Words That Improve Listening
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin diagnoses a common frustration: students who mentally check out and begin moving as soon as they think they understand directions, causing the teacher to lose them before finishing critical details. Reacting by raising one's voice or repeating information after the fact comes too late, and pausing awkwardly mid-direction, while better than pushing through, still interrupts flow and adds a negative vibe. His fix is a simple three-word phrase said before giving any directions: "in a moment," signaling clearly that more information is still coming and students shouldn't act yet. He claims the most effective teachers use the phrase up to a dozen times a day, and that its power compounds over time as it becomes a conditioned cue for students to keep listening rather than guess. The article closes by teasing a companion four-word phrase to be covered the following week.
points: Students often mentally and physically check out as soon as they think they understand directions, missing the remaining details.
The fix is a three-word cue said before giving directions: "in a moment," signaling explicitly that more information is coming.
The most effective teachers reportedly use the phrase up to a dozen times a day.
The phrase's effectiveness compounds over time, becoming a conditioned, near-automatic listening cue for students.
quotes: As soon as your students think they understand what you’re asking of them, they mentally check out.
In response, it’s common for teachers to increase the volume of their voice in an effort to cut through the fog.
A better way to handle it is to utter three simple words before giving directions.
The phrase is: “In a moment.” As in, “In a moment, we’re going to begin writing a response to the day’s reading.
It keeps students from moving on mentally or physically until you’ve finished giving every last direction.
The most effective teachers use the phrase up to a dozen times a day.
Eventually, active listening will become Pavlovian in response.
